doc.title: Michael Abene interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: No vacation from music; writing routine
summary: He can't take a vacation from music, describes European workshops, and his early-morning writing groove, and says he is never satisfied with old charts.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That’s hard. My wife should be here to answer that one. Not really. It’s very hard for me. Like when we do the workshops in Europe a lot of times we’re gone from the middle of June to the middle of August in Europe. And we try to combine some like quote hang time in there. But still you’re thinking about the next workshop. I probably think less — I don’t say I don’t entirely put it out of my head, I probably think less about things when I’m over in Europe. If I have a couple of days I probably think less. Because I know what’s going on in the next workshop, and I know what I’ve got is pretty much set. So I try to like kind of, for me anyway, cool out. For me. Which is not generally somebody else’s cooling out. But when I’m home, forget about it. There’s no way. In fact when I’m home, people say well you’re home, you’re not so busy. I say when I’m home I’m a hundred times busier. Because when I’m in Europe first of all I don’t — when I’m traveling I don’t do any composing at all. After you’re finished teaching or getting ready for concerts and rehearsing, the last thing you want to do is sit at a keyboard and write for ten or twelve hours. It’s the last thing you want to do. If you’re in these beautiful countries, you want to go hang and taste the food or the wines or whatever. The last thing you want to do is start writing. So the drag is when I get back though, it takes me a while to get back into that writing groove. That’s the hard part for me. And I know I come back and I see all that score paper I left on the piano. I purposely don’t touch anything. Whatever I’ve started, it’s laying there for like two months. And I come back and I tell them if you clean me, she knows better, don’t touch anything. And so now I try to start to find that groove again. Because it’s a groove. You really are in a groove. Even though like I say I teach four days a week, and very rarely do I have time to write in those four days. But once that weekend comes I’m up like maybe at four or five in the morning and I’m hitting it. And you know like years ago when you first started playing or on the scene you get home at four or five in the morning. So I don’t do that anymore. Now it’s like more or less a normal day. If I’m off from school I’m up at four or five, maybe six. And then I’m writing all day. So maybe I’ll stop for about an hour in the afternoon and cool out. So by eight or nine or ten o’clock I’ve been up like sixteen hours already man. I’m ready to pack it in. So then I’ll do the same thing again. But that’s the focus that it really takes to do that. You can’t — even if I come up with two good bars I’m thrilled. So it’s not the amount of music, it’s trying to, hopefully, in your own head, trying to keep the quality at a high level.
It sounds like your own personal standards are pretty high.

Yeah. And again, nobody bats a thousand. Everybody has their moments, oh man I should have just done that. Even somebody said, “I heard a chart you did thirty years ago.” I said, “I always wanted to go to another key over in that spot.” I always wonder. I should have changed this ending. Anyway, don’t talk to me about the old stuff. Don’t

even talk to me about the new stuff. And somebody’ll say to me, like if I finish a chart yesterday and somebody’ll say to me today, “well what were you thinking about?” I’ll say I could not tell you now how I came to certain inclusions maybe yesterday. Maybe if I sit and think about it. But sometimes when you finish a piece, it’s almost like your memory gets wiped for a minute. So sometimes when I go to do workshops and know I have to explain some music I will kind of go back to it and just listen to the recording of it and say okay, I’ve got to remind myself why I did this.
